If there is to be no such division of authority, if th& Dominion Government is not to expect the banks, the municipalities, or the Provincial Governments to take part in this matter, then it is for the Dominion Government to say so and to live up to its promises.
We do not wish to raise this question in any spirit of criticism or with any desire to hamper the Government, but to impress upon Parliament how important the question is from a national standpoint that the details of the matter should be worked out so that justice shall be done to all parties concerned, and that no part of the country and no section of the people shall fail of the assistance required because of lack of understanding between the different authorities concerned or in regard to the exercise of authority by this Government. And, I repeat, if a misunderstanding has existed, or exists up to the present time, it is because of the Government itself and not because of its critics.

I do not intervene to find the slightest fault with the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Roche). I should like to offer to him and to the Government my sympathy; and I would extend that sympathy to the people of the West. I offer to the Government my sympathy in their having to deal with a problem of such magnitude at a time when money is so scarce and the nation is taken up, as we all know, with an affair of overpowering size and importance outside our own boundaries. I have risen for the purpose of making one or two observations which I think may convey practical suggestions to the minister which he might find useful to consider and possibly to act upon. I have the good fortune to represent a constituency which is inhabited by a very large number of highly intelligent settlers. They have shown, their intelligence by coming to a part of the country where, in the thirteen years that I have known it, no large portion of the community has suffered by either hail or drought. I could mention other ways in which they have shown their intelligence, but refrain for the present. I have had, nevertheless, a couple of letters from limited areas in my constituency. One of these refers to a fact to which my hon. friend from Qu'Appelle (Mr. Thomson) al-

luded-that some people are in difficulties at the moment through having been" hailed out and not being insured. The other letter pointed out what is very well known to us all who live in the West, that it was a very dry year all 'over the western provinces. The drouth affected one limited portion, at any, rate, of even the Red Deer constituency, favourable though its location. Now, in the presence of these facts which I do not think can be gainsaid, I hope the Government has not followed too arbitrarily the line in defining what they understand to be the drouth-stricken area. If I followed the hon. Minister of the Interior correctly, he seemed to confine his promises to an area exclusively within the southern limits of Alberta, for example. That is what I understand him to mean by drouth-stricken area. I would therefore ask the minister in all sincerity to remember that there are isolated cases outside Southern Alberta of people who have been affected by the drouth, and there would appear to be no good reason why they should be arbitrarily excluded from the Minister's careful and, I trust, favourable consideration. I offer that suggestion sincerely and somewhat hopefully. As a matter of fact, while we may regard this question from the point of view of the settler with whom we all sympathize, yet in this House we ought to regard it very largely from the point of view of the results which are likely to be obtained. And I should like to point out to the minister that he would have a better guarantee of results for grain advanced in an area so generally successful in its crop as that which I have the honour to represent than he would in the southern district, where, I am afraid, drouth is rather frequent. I was reassured by the statement of my hon. friend from Medicine Hat (Mr. Buchanan) on that subject, but I have heard others say that the hot winds there are so prevalent, that a crop in four years is all that they can look for. I would suggest to the Minister that it might be a bad investment for a nation to put seed grain into that region. At any rate, I would suggest that it might be possible to make inquiries of the individual settlers who are being relieved to find how often they have been stricken by drouth. I sometimes have had a doubt whether the policy of what I might call pushing settlement, has not been carried too far in southern Alberta. I have often wondered whether it would not have been better if large areas 
in that region bad been left to be ranged by cattle. However that may be, I think it would be well worth the Minister's consideration whether he could not, through his numerous agents, institute inquiries in each case of relief, if possible, as to how far be >is likely to get results from advancing seed grain in specific cases and how often the people he is helping to put seed into the ground have been stricken with drouth in the years immediately past. To keep a man putting seed into an area that will only grow grain once in four years is of very questionable benefit either to the man or to the country.
That is one suggestion I should like to make. Then, I should like to be allowed to press the idea with which I opened-that the Minister might extend his idea of the drouth-stricken area, somewhat anyhow. I sympathize with him in the difficulties of the situation; they are- very great. The price of grain is a tremendous aggravation of the case and increases very much the difficulties of the Administration. Nevertheless, with a view to the results, I would press upon the Minister that he should not close his mind absolutely to isolated cases outside of what he appears to have regarded as the drouth-stricken area. If he opens his mind to this extent and wants to know where he can help some people outside of southern Alberta with the utmost certainty of good results, I shall be glad to tell him of one or two limited localities in the riding I have the honour to represent.

One would not be a loyal representative of any constituency of western Canada who did not feel very deeply concerned as to the situation of that country in regard to seed grain. Nor, indeed, could one endowed at all with human sympathy, no matter from what part he came, be doing his duty if he did not exercise it to the full in the extension of relief.
The hon. member who has just taken his seat has made remarks which we on this side of the House cannot but appreciate. We feel perhaps more keenly and directly than they the responsibility of the situation, particularly the financial difficulty involved. I rise not to add anything to what the Minister responsible has said or to the Government policy, but.only because the hon. member who has just sat down and hon. members who preceded him did not seem to fully comprehend the effect of the Minister's

statement. But I fear that, in the matters in which they were astray, if the Minister was not explicit'it is impossible for me to be more so. The occasion is fraught with unusual difficulty from several causes. In the first place the year before last in our country was not an auspicious year. The crops on the whole were bountiful, but only ordinarily so, in the districts most affected by the drouth of 1914; but the prices received were not proportionate to the cost involved. The prices were not equal to those received in previous years and this year. Following that a season of excessive drouth prevailed, extending from our own older province of Manitoba westerly to the Rockies, and most pronounced in the southern portions of Alberta and Saskatchewan. That was, of course, the initial, the foundation cause of the trouble. But upon that there was heaped this situation that at a time of financial depression caused not only by the war but by other conditions and intense indeed before the war commenced, the banks assumed an attitude that added indeed to the difficulties of the settlers; the banks assumed such an attitude, whether justifiably or not I cannot inquire, which has resulted in their not being of the assistance to the farmers that they have been in previous years and not being, in the opinion of a very great many, of the assistance that they ought to have been last year. The duties or responsibilities of the Government were great on account of both these conditions. However, in the province of Manitoba, from which I come, even this unusual situation was not such as to involve extraordinary responsibility upon this Government. It is a matter of congratulation to us from that province-and in this I am sure that I shall be joined by the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Cruise) and the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Molloy)-that even although we had suffered to a considerable extent from last year's drouth and although, as a result of that, there are large areas in that province to which assistance must undoubtedly be extended, an appeal to the Dominion Government is not yet essential in regard to patented lands. As to the two other provinces the situation is different. A similar situation arose there once before. As the minister has pointed out a drouth, although not to the same extent, occurred in 1908. That was met by the Government of the day by advances to the provinces, the provinces supplying the
grain to the settlers and becoming responsible to this Government. But so great and so fraught with difficulty was the situation this year that the remedy of 1908 could not be applied and it became necessary for this Government to extend the line further and to decide to what limit it could go, because it was determined to go to the utmost limit in the power of the Government in meeting the demands of the western settler. The Minister of the Interior has defined the line between the responsibilities of the Federal Government and the responsibilities of provincial governments and municipalities in those two provinces and I believe that we, representing the western provinces, should be grateful to the representatives on both sides of the House from all the provinces of Canada because no criticism has been made of the very liberal extension of the responsibilities assumed by this Government as compared with the responsibilities assumed by the Dominion Government in years gone by. We from the West believe, and I am sure that in this I shall be joined by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark), that the Government of the day has gone far and assumed a very great responsibility in carrying the line of demarcation as far as it has in regard to relief to the western settlers. Now how far has the line been carried? It is pointed out that when the situation first arose the Government of the day determined that there were certain areas that were so deeply involved and were so etriken that to those areas at least relief must be extended not only in the way of seed grain but in the way of supplies of the necessaries of life. Those areas were taken care of first, the unpatented lands and the patented lands, the unpatented, of course, being those for which this Government would be more directly responsible. But later on, as evidenced by a letter read by the hon. member for Regina, the Commissioner of Immigration at Winnipeg declared that the Government had decided to go further, to go beyond that stricken area. In this connection I have some fault to find with the hon. member for Regina (Mr. Martin), and I include in my complaint the hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Neely). I think I have discovered in the remarks of both these gentlemen one cause and a very great cause, for the added difficulties the Government is in, difficulties for which they are not responsible, but for which I am not so sure the hon. member for Regina is not responsible. The letter of the

Commissioner of Immigration of October 21, that has been so much discussed, is not worded, perhaps, as a lawyer would word it; but at all events its meaning is reasonably clear and its meaning in regard to the points referred to by the hon. member for Regina is perfectly clear. It will be remembered that the hon. member for Regina said that after reading that letter, after having had it shown to him by various farmers in his constituency, he assured them that in it no distinction was drawn and that, without respect to person, or area, the Government would give seed grain to any man who asked it. He assured them that they would he quite justified in selling their wheat because the Government of Canada had undertaken to be responsible for seed grain if they did not have it. Was he justified in giving that assurance to his constituents? What is there in the letter to justify it? Was he acting fairly with the Government of Canada or with his constituents? Does the letter say that the Government of this country would be responsible for seed grain to any man who was without it, whether on patented or unpatented lands? It says nothing of the kind. The letter is written after the Government has been catering to. the necessities of those who have lost their crop by drouth within certain specified areas. Under those circumstances the letter says:
In answer to your letter of recent date, asking for an advance of seed grain, I have to inform you that this department is making arrangements to supply bona fide settlers, who have lost their crop this year and are unable to obtain seed, with good clean seed next spring, delivery to start about the middle of February.
Then he goes on to say in a subsequent paragraph that the applicant should state in his letter whether his land is unpatented or patented, and if patented the encumbrances upon it. The hon. member for Regina went on to say that the Government was in an exceedingly generous mood at that time, and that they offered to advance this man seed grain no matter where he came from and what his condition, so long as he asked for it, and so long as he gave his note at 5 per cent. But did the Government offer there to give it to any mam who had not seed- grain?
5 p.tn. He had first to be a bona fide settler ; secondly, he had to be in the position that he had lost his crop in 1914, that he had not sold his crop; thirdly, he had to be, in the position that he could not obtain seed grain elsewhere.
IMr. Meighen.]

I did not say that I had ever advised any man to sell his grain. I said that by reason of this letter men had sold their grain, and that a reasonable interpretation of the letter was that the Government was supplying seed grain to any man in the prorvinces who had lost his crop, whether on patented or unpatented land and whether within the stricken area or not.

I am only too glad to receive the correction of the hon. member, because I recognize that his statement needed correction, and very badly needed it. The hon. member for Regina did say that many had come to him and said that they had sold their grain, and that he justified them in selling their grain and pointed to the Government's letter as making good to them the grain they had so sold. I say to the hon. member that he had no mandate and no warrant in that letter to make such a statement. The hon. member for Regina goes further. He says that the generosity of the Government was evidenced by the fact that they were willing to supply seed grain and to take nothing but an oath. Now, I draw his attention to the fact that Mr. Bruce Walker in the latter part of his letter states that the applicants must in their application state whether their land, if patented, is encumbered-it could not be encumbered if unpatented-and if encumbered, what encumbrances are against it. I ask the hon. member what would be the use of that information if we were not going to take a lien on the land?

How does the hon. gentleman explain the statement, that as far as patented lands are concerned the only security asked for in the application is the promissory note at 5 per cent payable on a certain date?

I answer, that is not in the letter. It does not say that that will be the only security asked for. It says, that will be asked for, and then says, tell us what encumbrances are against your land. I do not need to observe to the House that the hon. member for Regina has not yet answered my question as to what value to the commissioner the information would be as to whether the land was encumbered or not if they did not intend to have anything to do with the land. I earnestly hope that the hon. member for Regina was not joined by too many of his colleagues on that side of the House in

interpreting the contents of that letter to their constituents. It is a fact that, as a result of something, the applications for seed grain have come in very late and very precipitously. It is a fact that taking what care the Government could and making all investigations within its power, and, as the result of that care and those investigations, having procured such a supply of seed grain at a very moderate price as they felt	would be sufficient,
Notwithstanding that, later on and right up to the end of January, 1915, large numbers of applications poured in. I believe the Minister of the Interior said some 9,000. It may be there is some explanation of that. It may be that because of an industrious circulation of a wrong interpretation of the letter of October 21st, men in the province who had never hoped to look to the Government for assistance were induced to look for assistance at that late date, and that in consequence all these applications came in.
However, the main question now is what is the Government doing, where does the Government's responsibility end and where does the responsibility of others begin ? The hon. minister has stated-and it did not seem to be caught at all by the hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Neely)-that the Government was in no way restricting its responsibility geographically within those provinces. That is to say that the relief of the Government, in the way of seed grain and for feed for horses for putting in the seed, extended to places beyond the stricken area. The minister also stated the conditions under which that relief would be extended; that in cases beyond the stricken area where the farmer had suffered the previous year as the farmer in the drouth-stricken area had suffered, and where, as a result, he could not procure seed grain elsewhere, the Government was prepared in those cases to mete out to him the same relief as to the farmer of the stricken area. That is, wherever the farmer could place himself in the same position as to causes and conditions as., the farmer in the stricken area, then he placed himself in the same position as to remedy. I do not know that a fairer policy could be agreed upon. I do not think the hon. member for Red Deer or the hon. member for Edmonton will say that the line could possibly be drawn, having regard to the responsibility of precedent, more generously than it has been done. There is not a definition of locality; but the "causes must be the same, the conditions must be the same as to the possiblity of getting relief elsewhere, and, being the same, the farmer is in the same position as to remedy I do not wish to be understood as arguing that beyond the pale of the relief so extended there will not be many deserving cases, many eases such as those described by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, where the farmer though he may have had some remnant of a crop in 1914, had not grain of such a quality that he would dare to use it as seed in 1915. There may be" some cases such as that which are deserving cases; possibly just as deserving as those to which relief must be granted, 'but the line must be drawn somewhere and there are responsibilities upon other institutions, upon other governments, upon municipalities and units as well as upon this Government. And I believe all will agree that under the very unusual and overpowering circumstances of the time, when the calls upon the treasury of Canada are unprecedented, the Government has met the situation in a generous spirit, and in a spirit that every reasonable man should accept.

It was not my intention to say anything on this debate, because fortunately in my part of the province of Saskatchewan we had a fair crop. Up to the present I have not received a single letter from a constituent on the subject of seed grain. But it seems to me at this stage of the debate that there is some uncertainty about the position of the Government. The Solicitor General has explained it pretty well. We all know that he has a wonderful faculty of drawing nice distinctions in law or in anything else, but will the ordinary farmer who has not seed for his next crop be able to follow the nice distinctions in this letter that my hon. friend draws? Mr. Walker stated absolutely that those who were on patented lands would	be	asked for a note.
I do not think it is worth arguing about whether, in addition to that, they give security on their land or not. If the Government want additional security, well and good; -I think they are quite entitled to it. Here is the position: Farmers want seed grain; they were all led to believe by this letter of Mr. Walker's that they would get seed grain. I have a copy of Mr. Walker's letter, and there is absolutely nothing said in it about a restricted area. There is nothing said to the effect that it

will be confined to farmers who are living on homesteads the patents for which have not been issued. According to this letter any farmer on earth would be justified in saying that if he had lost his crop last year he could get seed grain from the Government. The Solicitor General says that the municipalities and the provincial governments must assume responsibility in the matter of seed grain. It is no time now to come forward and say that the municipalities and thfe provincial governments must assume responsibility for seed grain.
After the members of the provincial Government in Saskatchewan came down here last fall and had an interview with the members of this Government, they went home with the understanding, which was perfectly satisfactory to them, that they would attend to a certain amount of relief in the stricken area in the province of Saskatchewan, and they have expended over a million and a quarter of dollars in carrying out that work. They understood absolutely that the Dominion Government would attend to all -matters of seed grain, and that they were not going to be called upon in that connection. Members of this Government asked the members of the provincial Government if they would pass certain legislation which would give this Government the right to a first security for the amount of any seed grain that they advanced to the settlers. The Saskatchewan Government said they would be pleased to pass the necessary legislation; they are quite willing to do that to-day and will do it.
To come forward now and say that the provinces and municipalities must assume responsibility in connection with this seed grain is altogether unfair. Had the Governments of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta known last August, September or October that they were going to be called upon to provide seed grain, or if the municipalities had known that they wouM be required to assume this responsibility, it would have been an easy matter then to have secured the seed grain. Today, I doubt if it is an easy matter. On the other hand, it would be a most difficult matter for these authorities to secure the necessary seed grain. We ought to have a straight and definite statement from this Government that in all deserving cases it will undertake to supply seed grain. It is not a gift; it is only a loan of the money.
1 know it is a large sum, and I know that the Government have a falling revenue and tremendous expenses to meet otherwise, but

if they want to follow up the argument that they have been putting forward for the last six months in favour of increasing production, let me ask how they are going to increase production if they allow two or three million acres to go without seed. Seed must be procured in order that we may get the benefit of next year's crop. Where is the seed to come from? Taking into consideration this letter, copies of which Mr. Bruce Walker sent out by the thousand all over the country in October last, it is up to the Government to supply every deserving case, and I would like to have a statement from the Minister of the Interior as to whether they will do so. I understand the Solicitor General, acquiesced in by the Minister of the Interior, to say that outside of the restricted area, throughout Saskatchewan, Alberta or Manitoba, if there is any farmer in the position of a farmer in the stricken area, his case will be examined into, and if it is found that he lost his crop last year he will get seed grain. That is satisfactory as far as it goes But there will be many cases, such as were mentioned by my hon. friend from Qu'Appelle (Mr. Thomson), where they have had a certain amount of crop but where the grain is Absolutely unfit for seed. If it was absolutely unfit for seed the revenue that the farmer got from the crop will not enable him to buy good seed especially now when, I do not suppose, wheat could be delivered to the farmer under |2 a bushel, or perhaps $1.75, or $1.80.
I think the Minister of the Interior should give us a definite statement that they will not throw this responsibility on the municipalities or on the provincial governments. They are not in a position at the present time to secure millions of dollars to get the necessary seed grain to give to the farmers. They have no organization for that purpose. The Minister of the Interior and the Minister of Agriculture have an organization already handling this very subject. Why then divide the responsibility? The responsibility cannot be divided and have any success in handling this question. What is done has to be done by this Government. They have the organization, they are in shape to do it and if they have not the money they can get it much more easily than the provincial governments or the municipalities can.
I say again that this letter of Mr. Walker led every farmer in the country to believe that if he had not seed grain to sow the

land that he had ready <he could get it from the Government. It may be that, technically speaking, as was pointed out by the Solicitor General, there are some loopholes to enable you to place another interpretation upon this letter. But this Government have led the farmers to believe that they were going to give them seed grain if they did not have it. Take security for it if y,ou like, take a lien on the land and get the necessary guarantee from the provincial governmqjit to give your lien priority over all other encumbrances on the land-take or get that if you want to, but give the farmer the seed. If you do not give it to him he is not going to be able to get any seed grain. You have led him to believe that he would get it and if he does not get it the responsibility is on this Government and there will be the loss of many millions of dollars if we have not a good crop next year. It will be a severe loss because the price next fall, whether the war stops to-morrow or goes on a year or two, will be high. It is the duty of this Government to give seed grain to every farmer who has not got it otherwise, charge him the price of it and take the necessary security. This Government will not lose a dollar. They get their money back with five per cent interest. We heard the Minister of the Interior say what the banks were going to do. I quite agree with my hon. friend from Medicine Hat (Mr. Buchanan) that if they do what the Minister said they might do there will be a tremendous change in their policy. I doubt if they will do very much in advancing money to farmers. They have never done it in the past, and I think it would be a poor reed for the farmer who has no seed grain to rely upon. I do not think they will all get it if that is the case. This is a serious matter. The Government has spent millions of dollars on this question as it is and all we ask is that they may go a little farther and carry out exactly what everybody will naturally take to be the meaning of this letter that Mr. Bruce Walker sent out broadcast over the whole country- Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and Alberta-in which no distinction was made with reference to the restricted area. Take the security if you wish, but do not have divided responsibility, for it will not work, and it is too late if it did work. If you are going to make a success of 'his, the Federal Government will have to deal with the whole question of seed grain and if this Government does not take action in the light of this letter, they will be held
responsible by the people who are not able to get seed.

I rise
in the first place to express my appreciation of the attitude on this question taken by the members who come from the older provinces. Prima facie there is no duty on the Federal Government to supply seed grain for patented land in any province of Canada. That is clear. In the province of Ontario this Government is not asked to supply seed grain, nor yet is it asked to do so in the province of Quebec. For once I am entirely in accord with my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) when he says that this Government has approached this problem as one of great magnitude, recognizing that it is a question that must be dealt with in the very best possible way, having regard to the conditions that exist and to the precedents by which it is more or less bound.
Unfortunately, owing to causes about which it would not now be proper to inquire, the western provinces do not own their natural resources, and have, in my judgment, parted with them for a very insufficient compensation. Having regard to these ' conditions, the Federal Government having assumed responsibility for the administration of the public domain in these provinces, feels that in accordance with the precedent adopted in days gone by it should meet the existing situation and deal with it. That being so, the question as to what should be done in this particular case is a matter for consideration, and I am bound to say that I am very much reassured by the statement of the Minister of the Interior this afternoon. I did at one time feel owing to the documents to which attention has been directed this afternoon, that possibly some one had been misled or that there had been a change of policy on the part of the Administration. Such I now know is not the case. After all, it is no longer a theory but a condition that confronts us, and the question is as to how the Government is going to discharge the duty it has taken upon itself, in the light of the circular sent out to the settlers and which indicated that in so far as seed grain was concerned, the Administration proposed to supply seed grain solely within the stricken area, whether the settlers lived on patented or unpatented land. At first it was only supposed to be on unpatented land, their duty being only to homesteaders. But, in order

that their might not be divided authority within that area, the Government very properly assumed the duty of dealing with those who live on patented and unpatented land. I think they are dealing with the situation fairly, especially since the Minister of the Interior has announced that he was prepared to extend the same treatment to those who are similarly situated beyond that stricken area. I think he went as far as he possibly could, and I would like to adopt the language ol the member for Red Deer to this extent, that I hope the minister will not be too censorious or critical, but that where he finds areas that have been devastated by drouth or hail, he will extend to them the same treatment as he has to that area which is represented in this House by the hon. member for Lethbridge.
The condition is really a very serious one. Sometimes I think the members of this House who represent eastern constituencies little realize the conditions brought about in some parts of western Canada. In some districts the land has been swept as clean as a floor, and where once there was vegetation there is now nothing but the driest dust. It is even true that the children of the farmers in some instances have been suffering from the pangs of hunger, almost starvation, and under these circumstances the Government relief is absolutely needed to encourage the settlers within that area and to enable them to have their land bear crops next year. As the hon. gentleman from Macleod has said, we have had more snow and moisture this winter than we have had for many years, and I have every reason to believe that next year we will reap abundant harvests within that very area where in the past succeeding crop failures have occurred. Even if the Government should expend several millions more than was anticipated at first, it seems to me that this duty devolves upon them fairly. I think we in the West have every reason to feel grateful for the spirit of toleration with which hon. gentlemen who come from other provinces have dealt with this question in this time of great stress in the West.
Motion negatived.
